A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable, complete 15-page versions of iTool. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite retitling and presentation changes.

before.justification: v3 reports original BFCL and API-Bank evaluations, component ablations, training-data scaling experiments, and error analysis, including supplementary preference-optimization experiments.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark evaluations and supplementary experiments, with revised scores and component, curriculum, and iteration analyses.

M1.justification: The curriculum, replay-buffer sampling, MCTS rewards, and SimPO objectives remain the same. However, Section 3.2 changes its description of MCTS steps from tool calls or sentences to punctuation-terminated fragments such as argument assignments. The unchanged appendix examples do not resolve whether this changes the procedure or clarifies its earlier implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use ToolACE training data and evaluate BFCL Non-live, Live, Multi-turn, relevance/irrelevance detection, and API-Bank L1/L2. v4's simple/complex terminology refers to the existing Non-live/Live categories; no new task or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–2 and the appendix preference-algorithm comparison is unchanged. Within component analyses, v4 adds ordinary SFT to the module comparison, removes Mixed SFT from the curriculum plot, and removes the Base comparator from the MCTS plot.

E3.justification: Section 2.2 changes the stated ToolACE size from up to 10K to 100K samples while retaining percentage-based training allocations, substantially revising the documented experimental scale. The iteration sweep also extends from 0–5 to 0–7, and module evaluation becomes a staged, scenario-specific comparison. These are reported setting/design changes; the PDFs do not establish whether the dataset-size revision reflects a correction or different data use.

E4.justification: The central module-isolation study in v3 Figure 5 is replaced by the Base/SFT/warm-up/IRT comparison in v4 Table 3, losing the explicit without-warm-up condition. The curriculum study drops its Mixed SFT comparison and adds Live results; MCTS and scaling studies lose Non-live/Multi-turn breakdowns, while iteration sensitivity extends to seven iterations. This substantially revises the supporting analyses, although the error distribution and two preference-pair cases remain.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 5 displays error bars, whereas the replacement module analysis in v4 Table 3 reports point values only. Neither version explains those bars or reports repeated-run counts. The MCTS seed remains 42, and no confidence intervals or significance procedures are added.

E6.justification: Reported iTool BFCL Overall/Live scores change from 62.92/76.82 to 63.26/78.29, and API-Bank L1/L2 from 77.34/51.83 to 78.89/52.87. The latter moves iTool above GPT-3.5-turbo-0125's unchanged 52.59 on L2. Other base-model scores and analysis curves also change, including appendix SimPO results. These are revised reported outcomes; the changed training-data description prevents assuming matched training conditions.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11 and the appendix preference-optimization objectives retain the same mathematical content. Neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs. The new difficulty thresholds document implementation criteria rather than a new theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract replaces approximately 12% better performance over baselines with 13.11% over the same-size base model and adds a 6.5% complex-scenario claim, corresponding to the Multi-turn difference from SFT. The central contribution remains iterative, deficiency-targeted tool learning using MCTS and preference optimization.

C2.justification: v4 softens the attribution of training-gain decay to insufficient diversity, changes the module interpretation from warm-up's greater importance to scenario-specific incremental benefits, and removes the warning about sacrificing simpler tasks. Section 7 also removes optimistic extrapolation to larger models while retaining computational and single-training-dataset limitations.

D1.justification: v4 supplies explicit easy/medium/hard thresholds in Section 3.1 and termination-character instructions in Section 3.2. v3 lists the difficulty factors without these cutoffs. Appendix B retains the same LoRA/QLoRA settings, learning rates, epochs, hardware, runtime, preference filtering, and MCTS parameters.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations including Li's agent-paradigm review, adaptive tool use, Luo's self-training work, Singh's agentic reasoning work, and TL-training. Octopus and LLM4EDA disappear from the references. Section 5's substantive positioning remains largely unchanged; removing the duplicate ReFT reference does not remove that research connection.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, preliminary-study explanation, experimental discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting around complex scenarios and response-fragment deficiencies. Author/header text and Appendix C's organization also change, although the main section sequence remains stable.

P2.justification: The module-ablation chart becomes Table 3, and the curriculum, MCTS, iteration, and data-scaling figures are substantially redesigned with different panels, legends, annotations, and displayed comparisons. Appendix C loses the standalone weather-tool example table; both preference-pair tables and the MCTS example diagram remain.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful implementation details and scenario-specific component results. However, it removes direct ablation controls and introduces reporting inconsistencies: Table 3 mixes percentage-point differences with relative percentages, and Section 4.3.3 still gives Qwen's score as 63.22 although Table 4 now reports 63.93; v3's text and table agreed. These losses in experimental interpretability and internal consistency outweigh the limited documentation gains, while the central study remains intact.
